doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

chapter: Big breaks: New Wave, Maynard, Tony Bennett
title: Backing vocalists: Rosemary Clooney and Mark Murphy
summary: He describes accompanying Rosemary Clooney and learning from Mark Murphy to enhance a singer without crowding.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: That’s a time you’ll never forget in your life. Never, ever. I was high as a kite. I felt extraordinarily good. And it was difficult, like backing up Ella, Nancy Wilson, a couple of other people, there was those points in time when you get up to blow and — not that long ago, five years ago, when I did Rosemary Clooney with Sam Noto, the two of us with Joe Coccuzo and all the cats from New York, we did it at the Art Park, and I was on tenor on that gig and we were in a rehearsal and we started to blow and read through the tunes and do the stuff and then I get to the soloing behind her or with her, whatever the case may be, and she turns around and says, “You’ve been with me my whole life.”

Like cool. I’m doing the gig. And that’s exactly what you want to know. That vocalist feels comfortable. She feels like she’s in her element because I’m playing the style of the chart. That’s another thing I’ve done my whole life.
Yeah well that takes a lot of musicality.

I don’t try and just blow arbitrarily because I’m a cool jazz player and I can play outside so I’m going to play that way on her chart. If you hired me you hired me to play the way I play. I play the chart the way the chart feels, the era, writer, the mood, the vocalist, that’s the way you try and interpret a chart. That’s the important way to play. And so you draw on a lot from that. I mean I had all the years of listening to cats blow, Ben Webster, all the different guys. If you’re going to play the right way on the thing, when she’s got a sexy little ballad that she wants to sing and she wants that mood set for her, and also Mark Murphy taught me a long time ago, I used to sit in with Mark because he used to play here in Buffalo, this is like a second home to him. And Mark would let me sit in. And Mark, you can’t just like try and blow in the spaces because Mark fills them in. He fills in — he’s a horn player as much as a vocalist, so you learn how to stay out of the way but enhance the melody. Sometimes it’s a counter line — instead of trying to blow, just a new melody that sits underneath and just gives him, like orchestrators do. So when I back up a vocalist that’s the kind of way I try and interpret. I don’t just try and stick in jock licks, rather to try and become part of the composite. And she dug it a lot. We had a great time that night, just a super time that night. So I mean there has been different things that I would say are the breaks. Getting the gig with Maynard, that was like I was elated. Absolutely elated. And I was happy as hell. I ended up to be his road manager for three of the four years that I was with him, and did a lot for him that way too.
